## Chapter Summary

Many analytical questions need more than grouping. A CASE expression classifies each row by conditions tested in order, and its ELSE decides what happens to rows that meet none of them; the simple form compares one expression with a list of values, and never matches NULL. SQLite stores dates as text, and its date functions work on that text. strftime formats a date into a period such as a year and month, and date moves a date with modifiers, applied in order, such as start of month; `'start of month', '+1 month', '-1 day'` gives a month's last day. julianday turns a date into a number of days, so that the difference between two dates is a subtraction. Date functions return text, except julianday, so their results must be compared with text or converted with CAST. Placed inside an aggregate, CASE turns categories into columns, which is conditional aggregation, the SQL counterpart of SUMIFS and of a PivotTable.

A window function calculates across a set of rows but keeps every row. `OVER ()` makes the window the whole result, PARTITION BY divides the rows into groups without collapsing them, and ORDER BY sets their order and, for an aggregate, makes a running total whose default window includes tied rows. A frame such as ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW decides which rows each calculation uses, and it counts rows, not months, so it needs one row for every month. The WINDOW clause names a window that several functions share. Ranking functions, such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK, number the rows and treat ties differently. LAG and LEAD return values from earlier and later rows, and LAG partitioned by the month compares each month with the same month a year before. Window functions are calculated with the SELECT list, after grouping, so they can work on grouped results, but neither WHERE nor HAVING can filter on them without a derived table or a common table expression.

A common table expression names a subquery at the start of a query with WITH, so that a long analysis reads as a series of steps that can each be checked on their own, and a one-row CTE can hold a query's parameters. A view saves a query in the database under a name. It stores the query rather than its result, so it always reflects the current data; a script drops it and creates it again to change it, and it is written only into the working copy, never into the downloaded file.

Applied to the controller's questions, these tools produced a monthly measure of direct, indirect, and total labor hours per standard hour, with the share of overtime, smoothed over a trailing twelve months, matched to the days that the time records cover, and saved as a view. The payroll classified with CASE tied to the ledger's charge to the cent. Indirect time appears in the records from the middle of 2024 and has been roughly flat since the middle of 2025, while direct hours per standard hour and the overtime share of direct labor kept rising through fiscal 2026. The largest months of the gap in account 1090 turned out to be months with three pay dates, because payroll is recorded when it is paid. Work orders took more than twice as long to complete. The ranking of work centers also exposed a pattern in the time records: far more hours than planned at the end of the routing, and far fewer at its start, while the plant as a whole stayed within plan. That pattern is for the auditors of Chapter 12 to test.
